title: God's grandeur (Hopkins)
hookLine: the world is charged with the grandeur of God; the Holy Ghost broods with warm breast
tomorrow: how small can a thing be and still be worth loving?

lines: A WORLD THAT LOOKS USED UP.
cards: Some weeks the world looks used up. Same parking lot, same gray sky, the same feed refreshed until it's numb. Is anything still holy in a world that worn?
Gerard Manley Hopkins answers in his first line: “The world is charged with the grandeur of God.” Charged, like a battery. Like the air before a storm.
It will flame out, he says, like shining from shook foil.

teach.b: Hopkins, a Jesuit priest and a poet, says yes, and he doesn't dodge the wear.

Generations have trod, have trod, have trod, he writes; all is seared with trade and smeared with toil, and the foot, in its shoe, can't even feel the soil. Then: “There lives the dearest freshness deep down things.”
Morning still springs up in the east after the last light leaves the west. Why?
Because the Holy Ghost over the bent world broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings. Brooding is what a bird does on a nest: warmth, patience, life underneath.

Some readers hear Genesis there, where “the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.” Worn, and charged, both at once. A neighbor tradition has its own words for the world pointing past itself.
The Qur'an speaks of the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, and calls them signs, ayat, for people of understanding.
A Muslim reading a sunrise as a sign and Hopkins watching foil flash are both looking at the world as more than it seems. The difference is real, and worth saying plainly.
Hopkins names the Holy Ghost, the Spirit of the Christian Trinity, brooding over the world.
The Qur'an teaches that God is one, with no partner, and its signs point beyond themselves to their one Maker. Shared wonder at night and day; different words for who stands behind it.

how: Some Christians read Hopkins's poem aloud and slowly, sometimes outdoors, sometimes alongside a psalm of creation.

o: Hopkins's poem: a worn world still charged with God
a psalm praising the size of the mountains and seas
a hymn about the glory of kings and great cathedrals

games.q: what the poem says — tap the pairs.
p: like a battery, about to spark

s: Hopkins thought the world was in perfect shape
he names the wear: trod, seared with trade, smeared with toil. and still, charged.
God's Grandeur is a nature poem, and God is only a figure of speech
it ends on the Holy Ghost brooding over the bent world.
in the poem, the Holy Ghost broods over the world like a bird on a nest
with warm breast and with ah! bright wings.

games.q: a friend from a Muslim family says the Qur'an calls night and day signs. what does that share with Hopkins, and where do they differ?
o: both read the world as pointing past itself; Hopkins names the Trinity's Spirit, the Qur'an God as one.
they say exactly the same thing, so the difference doesn't really matter.
Hopkins means nature itself is God; the Qur'an means nature is only matter.
games.why: shared: wonder at the world as a pointer beyond itself. different: Hopkins's Holy Ghost, and the Qur'an's one God with no partner. neither is ranked.

practice: Go to a window or step outside, and find one ordinary, worn thing: a cracked step, a puddle, a scuffed wall with light on it. Look at it for the whole sit without trading it for anything grander.
Wait for the moment it seems charged, the way foil flashes when it's shaken.

wordCard.voice: God's grandeur. Hopkins's poem: a worn world, still charged, with the Holy Ghost brooding over it.

orig.note: the Hebrew verb in Genesis 1:2 for the Spirit moving over the waters; some readers hear it in Hopkins's brooding.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: charged with grandeur. Worn and charged, both at once. That's sixteen seventy-two.
